Multi-year investment can be passed by setting the argument
``multi_investment_periods`` when calling the
``n.optimize(multi_investment_periods=True)``. For the pathway
optimisation ``snapshots`` have to be a pandas.MultiIndex, with the first level
as a subset of the investment periods.
The investment periods are defined in the component ``investment_periods``.
They have to be integer and increasing (e.g. ``[2020, 2030, 2040, 2050]``).
The investment periods can be weighted both in time called ``years``
(e.g. for global constraints such as :math:`\mathrm{CO}_2` emissions) and in the objective function
``objective`` (e.g. for a social discount rate) using the
``investment_period_weightings``.
The objective function is then expressed by
.. math::
\min \sum_{a \in A} w^o_a [\sum_{s | b_s<=a<b_s+L_s} (c_{s,a} G_s + \sum_t w^\tau_{a,t} o_{s,a,t}g_{s,a,t})]  .
Where :math:`A` are the investment periods, :math:`w^o_a` the objective weighting of the investment period, :math:`b_s` is the build year of an
asset :math:`s` with lifetime :math:`L_s`, :math:`c_{s,a}` the annualised
investment costs, :math:`o_{s,a, t}` the operational costs and :math:`w^\tau_{s,a}`
the temporal weightings (including snapshot objective weightings and investment
period temporal weightings).
The general procedure for modelling multi-investment periods in PyPSA is to add
an asset for each investment period, in which its capacity should be expandable.
For example, if you want to optimise onshore wind development in the period 2025-2040
with investment periods every 5 years, you add a generator with a corresponding
construction year and lifetime for each investment period

Multi-year investment can be passed by setting the argument
``multi_investment_periods`` when calling the
``n.optimize(multi_investment_periods=True)``. For the pathway
optimisation ``snapshots`` have to be a pandas.MultiIndex, with the first level
as a subset of the investment periods.

The investment periods are defined in the component ``investment_periods``.
They have to be integer and increasing (e.g. ``[2020, 2030, 2040, 2050]``).
The investment periods can be weighted both in time called ``years``
(e.g. for global constraints such as :math:`\mathrm{CO}_2` emissions) and in the objective function
``objective`` (e.g. for a social discount rate) using the
``investment_period_weightings``.

The objective function is then expressed by

.. math::
   \min \sum_{a \in A} w^o_a [\sum_{s | b_s<=a<b_s+L_s} (c_{s,a} G_s + \sum_t w^\tau_{a,t} o_{s,a,t}g_{s,a,t})]  .

Where :math:`A` are the investment periods, :math:`w^o_a` the objective weighting of the investment period, :math:`b_s` is the build year of an
asset :math:`s` with lifetime :math:`L_s`, :math:`c_{s,a}` the annualised
investment costs, :math:`o_{s,a, t}` the operational costs and :math:`w^\tau_{s,a}`
the temporal weightings (including snapshot objective weightings and investment
period temporal weightings).

The general procedure for modelling multi-investment periods in PyPSA is to add
an asset for each investment period, in which its capacity should be expandable.
For example, if you want to optimise onshore wind development in the period 2025-2040
with investment periods every 5 years, you add a generator with a corresponding
construction year and lifetime for each investment period

This allows one to specify different technological assumptions for the respective
investment period (for example, decreasing investment costs, increasing efficiencies,
improved capacity factors due to higher hub heights of wind turbines, extended lifetimes).
The generators are only available for use after the year of construction and before
the end of their lifetime, for example, the onwind-2030 generator built in 2030
cannot contribute to electricity generation in the 2025 investment period.
To ensure that the technical potential for onshore wind in the region is not
exceeded by the 4 onshore wind generators in our example, one has to add an
additional global constraint (``type=tech_capacity_expansion_limit``, see further description above).

The storage nominal power is given by :math:`\bar{h}_{n,s}`.
In contrast to the generator, which has one time-dependent variable, each storage unit has three:
The storage dispatch :math:`h_{n,s,t}` (when it depletes the state of charge):
.. math::
0 \leq h_{n,s,t} \leq \bar{h}_{n,s}
The storage uptake :math:`f_{n,s,t}` (when it increases the state of charge):
.. math::
0 \leq f_{n,s,t} \leq  \bar{h}_{n,s}
and the state of charge itself:
.. math::
0\leq soc_{n,s,t} \leq r_{n,s} \bar{h}_{n,s}
where :math:`r_{n,s}` is the number of hours at nominal power that fill the state of charge.
The variables are related by
.. math::
soc_{n,s,t} = \eta_{\textrm{stand};n,s}^{w_t} soc_{n,s,t-1} + \eta_{\textrm{store};n,s} w_t f_{n,s,t} -  \eta^{-1}_{\textrm{dispatch};n,s} w_t h_{n,s,t} + w_t\textrm{inflow}_{n,s,t} - w_t\textrm{spillage}_{n,s,t}
:math:`\eta_{\textrm{stand};n,s}` is the standing losses dues to
e.g. thermal losses for thermal
storage. :math:`\eta_{\textrm{store};n,s}` and
:math:`\eta_{\textrm{dispatch};n,s}` are the efficiency losses for
power going into and out of the storage unit.
There are two options for specifying the initial state of charge :math:`soc_{n,s,t=-1}`: you can set
``n.storage_units.cyclic_state_of_charge = False`` (the default) and the value of
``n.storage_units.state_of_charge_initial`` in MWh; or you can set
``n.storage_units.cyclic_state_of_charge = True`` and then
the optimisation assumes :math:`soc_{n,s,t=-1} = soc_{n,s,t=|T|-1}`.
If in the time series ``n.storage_units_t.state_of_charge_set`` there are
values which are not NaNs, then it will be assumed that these are
fixed state of charges desired for that time :math:`t` and these will
be added as extra constraints. (A possible usage case would be a
storage unit where the state of charge must empty every day.)
Store constraints
------------------
Store nominal energy and dispatch for each snapshot may be optimised.
The store nominal energy is given by :math:`\bar{e}_{n,s}`.
The store has two time-dependent variables:
The store dispatch :math:`h_{n,s,t}`:
.. math::
-\infty \leq h_{n,s,t} \leq +\infty
and the energy:
.. math::
\tilde{e}_{n,s} \leq e_{n,s,t} \leq \bar{e}_{n,s}
The variables are related by
.. math::
e_{n,s,t} = \eta_{\textrm{stand};n,s}^{w_t} e_{n,s,t-1} - w_t h_{n,s,t}
:math:`\eta_{\textrm{stand};n,s}` is the standing losses dues to
e.g. thermal losses for thermal
storage.
There are two options for specifying the initial energy
:math:`e_{n,s,t=-1}`: you can set
``n.stores.e_cyclic = False`` (the default) and the
value of ``n.stores.e_initial`` in MWh; or you can
set ``n.stores.e_cyclic = True`` and then the
optimisation assumes :math:`e_{n,s,t=-1} = e_{n,s,t=|T|-1}`.

"""Tests for storage boundary conditions across multiple investment periods.

Covers stores and storage units when snapshots are a period/timestep
MultiIndex. For each combination of the per-period cyclic flag and the
per-period initial flag, the boundary condition at the start of an investment
period must follow the documented storage models:

- per-period cyclic (``e_cyclic_per_period``/``cyclic_state_of_charge_per_period``,
  default ``True``): the level at the first snapshot of each investment period
  is linked to the *last snapshot of the same period* (wrap-around). The
  initial value (``e_initial``/``state_of_charge_initial``) is not its
  predecessor and is ignored for that asset.
- per-period initial (``e_initial_per_period``/
  ``state_of_charge_initial_per_period``): the level at the first snapshot of
  each investment period is reset to the initial value.
- both flags ``False``: the level continues chronologically across period
  boundaries and the initial value applies only before the very first
  snapshot of the horizon.

A default store or storage unit has per-period cyclic constraints switched
on, so adding an initial value must not make the level restart from that
initial value at every period start (which fabricates energy at every
planning-epoch boundary).
"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import pytest

import pypsa

PERIODS = [2020, 2030]
TIMESTEPS = ["t0", "t1", "t2"]
LOAD = [2.0, 1.0, 3.0, 1.5, 2.5, 2.0]
SOLVER = dict(solver_name="highs", solver_options={"output_flag": False})


def component_kwargs(kind, **kwargs):
    """Map neutral capacity/initial arguments to component-specific ones."""
    capacity = kwargs.get("capacity")
    initial = kwargs.get("initial")
    if kind == "Store":
        mapped = {"e_nom": capacity, "e_initial": initial}
        flags = {
            "cyclic_pp": "e_cyclic_per_period",
            "initial_pp": "e_initial_per_period",
        }
    else:
        mapped = {"p_nom": capacity, "max_hours": 1, "state_of_charge_initial": initial}
        flags = {
            "cyclic_pp": "cyclic_state_of_charge_per_period",
            "initial_pp": "state_of_charge_initial_per_period",
        }
    for neutral, actual in flags.items():
        if neutral in kwargs:
            mapped[actual] = kwargs[neutral]
    return mapped


def level_series(n, kind):
    if kind == "Store":
        return n.stores_t.e["storage"].to_numpy()
    return n.storage_units_t.state_of_charge["storage"].to_numpy()


def build_network(kind, with_generator=False, **kwargs):
    n = pypsa.Network()
    snapshots = pd.MultiIndex.from_product(
        [PERIODS, TIMESTEPS], names=["period", "timestep"]
    )
    n.snapshots = snapshots
    n.add("Bus", "bus")
    n.add("Load", "load", bus="bus", p_set=LOAD)
    if with_generator:
        n.add("Generator", "gen", bus="bus", p_nom=10, marginal_cost=0.01)
    n.add(
        kind,
        "storage",
        bus="bus",
        marginal_cost=1.0,
        **component_kwargs(kind, **kwargs),
    )
    return n


@pytest.mark.parametrize("kind", ["Store", "StorageUnit"])
def test_cyclic_per_period_governs_boundary_over_initial(kind):
    """Per-period cyclic storage with an initial value wraps within each period.

    With cheap generation available, the optimal storage level stays well
    below the initial value at every period start instead of restarting from
    it. (Before the fix, the level at the second period start was
    ``initial - LOAD[0]`` and chronology across the boundary was broken.)
    """
    n = build_network(kind, with_generator=True, capacity=9, initial=9)
    status, condition = n.optimize(**SOLVER)
    assert status == "ok"
    level = level_series(n, kind)
    steps_per_period = len(TIMESTEPS)
    assert level[steps_per_period] < 0.5
    # the boundary transition reflects operation, not a jump to the initial value
    assert level[steps_per_period] - level[steps_per_period - 1] < 0.5


@pytest.mark.parametrize("kind", ["Store", "StorageUnit"])
def test_cyclic_per_period_cannot_be_fed_by_initial_value(kind):
    """A per-period cyclic store with net outflow and no source is infeasible.

    The initial value may not be injected at every period start to close the
    cycle; the model must report the inconsistency instead.
    """
    n = build_network(kind, capacity=9, initial=9)
    status, condition = n.optimize(**SOLVER)
    assert status != "ok"
    assert condition == "infeasible"


@pytest.mark.parametrize("kind", ["Store", "StorageUnit"])
def test_initial_per_period_restarts_each_period(kind):
    """With the per-period initial flag, each period restarts from the initial value."""
    n = build_network(kind, capacity=9, initial=9, cyclic_pp=False, initial_pp=True)
    status, condition = n.optimize(**SOLVER)
    assert status == "ok"
    level = level_series(n, kind)
    expected_first = 9 - np.cumsum(LOAD[:3])
    expected_second = 9 - np.cumsum(LOAD[3:])
    np.testing.assert_allclose(level, [*expected_first, *expected_second])


@pytest.mark.parametrize("kind", ["Store", "StorageUnit"])
def test_without_per_period_flags_state_continues_across_periods(kind):
    """Without per-period flags the level is chronological; initial counts once."""
    n = build_network(kind, capacity=20, initial=13, cyclic_pp=False, initial_pp=False)
    status, condition = n.optimize(**SOLVER)
    assert status == "ok"
    level = level_series(n, kind)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(level, 13 - np.cumsum(LOAD))
    steps_per_period = len(TIMESTEPS)
    assert level[steps_per_period] - level[steps_per_period - 1] == pytest.approx(
        -LOAD[steps_per_period]
    )

That mask re-included the per-period wrap based on the **global** cyclic flag (`e_cyclic` / `cyclic_state_of_charge`) instead of the **per-period** flag (`e_cyclic_per_period` / `cyclic_state_of_charge_per_period`, both default `True`).

For a default store/storage unit carrying `e_initial`/`state_of_charge_initial`, the wrap predecessor was dropped and `rhs = -e_initial` was applied at *every* investment-period start — the code silently behaved as if `e_initial_per_period=True`, injecting energy at each planning-epoch boundary. - per-period cyclic set (with or without an initial value): each period wraps — cyclic governs the boundary; the initial state is not its predecessor;
- per-period initial set: each period restarts from the initial value;
